1. The animation compares the total interest on a mortgage across three setups. A 30-year loan on its own schedule costs $477,622 in interest. The same 30-year loan paid off in 15 years costs $210,691. A true 15-year loan costs $189,069. The idea is that paying a loan off faster cuts the interest a lot, and that a 15-year loan has a lower rate than a 30-year loan. Frames 3–6 show a character named Tessa, labeled "ILLUSTRATIVE", standing by a house. Next to the house is a gold stack, probably cash or savings. Beside that are two pale pillars, which may be a second pile of money or an investment.

2. In frames 1–2, the tall green stacks of interest shrink from the 30-year schedule to the 15-year versions. The camera also zooms in on the comparison. In frames 3–6 the scene switches to Tessa and her house. The gold stack stays about the same, while the pale pillars and some small gray blocks shift in height and position. In frame 6, dark panels and small blocks appear near the house, but the image doesn't make clear what they stand for.

3. It means that paying the mortgage off early saves roughly $267,000 in interest compared with the full 30-year schedule. Even compared with the 30-year loan paid in 15 years, a true 15-year loan saves about $21,600. The Freddie Mac survey is the source of the rates. The footer says "US only · history, not a forecast." So the numbers are past data, and the pale pillars may be showing what investing could do, though the frames don't say so.

4. The image gives no explicit advice. A viewer might take away that paying extra toward a mortgage saves a lot of interest. The Tessa frames hint at weighing that against putting the money elsewhere. Nothing on screen says which one to choose.

5. The animation didn't state any advice. The idea that extra payments save interest comes from the labeled dollar figures in frames 1–2. My reading of the Tessa frames as a "pay down vs. invest" tradeoff is my own conclusion, since those frames have no figures or labels explaining the pillars.
